name: Gareth Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to give me both the public version and the private one. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the junior house drummer at Northgate Sound, which is a recording studio that does pop demos, podcasts and a lot of band records. Most days I'm in by ten, tuning the kit in Room B, and I play on whatever's booked: a singer's demo, a band whose drummer can't keep time, a jingle. Three evenings a week I teach kids at the Beat Academy above the music shop on Station Road. The best bit is when a song suddenly locks in; the worst is eight hours of playing to a click track with headphones squeezing my skull.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And money? How secure do you feel?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Better than most drummers I know. The studio pays me a day rate that's high for someone as green as me, because Marcus (the studio owner) likes having a drummer on call. Priya (my girlfriend) is a maths teacher, we bought a small flat last year, and I've still got about eight months of my wages saved. I use AI now and then, mostly to turn a recording into a drum chart when I'm lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a nice tool and nothing more, like when everyone panicked about drum machines in the eighties. Real drummers are still getting booked, and I'd say that at the studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life carries on, which I'm happy with. I'm still not great at the job, so the thing that could cost me sessions is a better drummer moving to town. AI wouldn't be the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my studio days and my three teaching nights. I'd use the chart app a bit more to save prep time, and put money into lessons with a jazz drummer, Lou, to get my brushes and feel up. We'd keep paying the flat down a bit faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed. That's the world I'm in now and I quite like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a better drummer moving to town is the real threat. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year a drummer from a big touring band moved here and Marcus (the studio owner) booked him for two albums I wanted. I sulked for a week. Then I booked lessons. That's how I ended up with Lou.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything you do at the studio get automated in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the editing. The engineer spends ages lining my hits up to the grid, and software would do that faster. That's his time, though, not mine.

say: AI is a **nice tool**, like drum machines were in the eighties.
Real drummers like me are **still getting booked** at the studio.
think: The real threat is a **better drummer** moving to town, not AI.
I'm still **not great** yet, so my playing matters more than technology.
do: Keep my **studio days** and three teaching nights at the Beat Academy.
Use the **chart app** more to save lesson-prep time.
Pay for lessons with **Lou**, a jazz drummer, and overpay the flat.
feel: **Relaxed**, because this world is the one he already lives in.
S0.quote: Last year a drummer from a big touring band moved here and Marcus (the studio owner) booked him for two albums I wanted. I sulked for a week.
fieldNote: His fear is **competition**, and he answers it by paying for better teaching.
He uses AI for **small chores** and sees no threat in that.
A shared **mortgage** with a teacher partner gives him real ground under his feet.

steps.text: Keep playing studio days at Northgate Sound and teaching three nights
Pay for jazz lessons with Lou to improve brushes and feel
Overpay the flat mortgage a little each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the studio I'd say we need rules on AI music, like the union's been asking for: labels on fake tracks and pay for musicians whose playing trained the systems. Online I'd share that and keep it polite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, demos are the first thing to go. A singer who used to pay me a day rate to drum on a demo will just type in what they want and get a decent groove. Marcus would keep the band records for a while, but I reckon half my studio days disappear in two or three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Marcus this winter and ask what the studio's plan is. Once other drummers start using the AI groove tools properly, I'd learn them too, so I'm the guy who can fix a fake drum part and make it human. And I'd add a fourth teaching night at the academy, because kids still want a real person showing them a paradiddle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, then a bit sick, honestly. I like the studio more than the teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the money if half the studio days go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be okay on Priya's salary and my teaching, but it would hurt. I'd stop putting extra on the flat and keep the savings as savings. No new cymbals for a while, which sounds small but that's my one treat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides whether this is good or bad, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies selling these tools decided for us, and they didn't ask anyone who plays. I'm not against the tech. I just think if it's built on our recordings, some of the money should come back to musicians.

say: We need **labels** on AI tracks and pay for musicians whose playing trained them.
I'd share the **union's call** online and keep it polite.
think: **Demo work** goes first, because singers can just type in a groove.
About **half my studio days** could disappear within two or three years.
do: Ask Marcus about the **studio's plan** this winter.
Learn the **AI groove tools** once other drummers do, to fix fake parts.
Add a **fourth teaching night** at the Beat Academy.
feel: **Uneasy**, then a bit sick, because he prefers studio work to teaching.
S1.quote: A singer who used to pay me a day rate to drum on a demo will just type in what they want and get a decent groove.
fieldNote: He expects to lose **half** of his favourite work and picks the less loved fallback.
He'll adopt tools only **once proven** by others, true to his steady style.
He blames the **tech companies** for deciding without musicians, not the tech itself.

steps.text: Learn AI groove tools to fix and humanise fake drum parts
Add a fourth teaching night at the Beat Academy
Stop extra mortgage payments and hold savings as a cushion
Back the union's call for labels and pay for training data

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a proper political answer: tax the AI companies and pay people a basic income while everyone works out what's next. I'd say it at the studio, to my mates, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2028 my studio job is finished. Recording is all screens and files, and AGI does that end to end. The live drumming and teaching last until the robots arrive in 2031, so I'd have three years of gigs and kids and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd get into a working band that plays weddings and corporate parties, because people still want a drummer in the room. I'd keep teaching as many nights as I can. Priya and I would put the flat overpayments back on, to clear as much mortgage as possible before 2031, and I'd vote for whoever promises a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted. Like the floor tilted, and I'm only 27.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do those three years between 2028 and the robots mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're a runway, not a home. I'd use them to save and to work out a skill that needs a person, maybe running workshops in schools. But two years of warning first isn't much when you're still learning the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my girlfriend Priya that we'd be living on her salary sooner than we planned. Then I'd ask her if teachers are safe. I'm not sure what she'd say.

say: We need to **tax AI companies** and fund a basic income.
Everyone deserves time to work out **what's next**, not just a shrug.
think: My **studio job** is finished by 2028, because recording is all screens.
Live drumming and teaching last only until **robots in 2031**.
do: Join a **wedding and party band** that still wants a live drummer.
Teach as **many nights** as the academy can give him.
Restart **overpaying the flat** to cut the mortgage before 2031.
feel: **Gutted**, like the floor tilted when he's only 27.
S2.quote: I'd tell my girlfriend Priya that we'd be living on her salary sooner than we planned.
fieldNote: He sees **2028 to 2031** as a runway, not somewhere to stay.
His politics turn concrete: **basic income** and a tax on AI firms.
He leans on **Priya's salary**, and is unsure whether teaching is safe either.

steps.text: Join a wedding and corporate party band as its drummer
Teach every available night at the Beat Academy
Restart overpaying the mortgage to shrink it before 2031
Vote for parties promising a basic income and AI tax

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if governments start now, and I'd push for that. I'd tell the guys at the studio to start thinking about what they'd do instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is a decent run. I'd watch what the better drummers do and copy whatever works. By 2031 I want to be teaching properly, with a qualification, not just someone the kids' parents found online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year I'd start a part-time music teaching qualification, two evenings a week. I'd keep the studio days while they last and use the AI tools a bit, once Marcus sets them up. And we'd build the savings to a full year of both our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steadier. It's like seeing a storm two days out instead of when it's overhead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the studio would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo (the studio engineer) has spent fifteen years learning to mix, and mixing is the first thing AGI does well. She's 44 with no backup. I'd tell her to start teaching too, but she'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said copy whatever works. Is there a risk you wait too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's my habit. Priya says I wait until everyone's done it and then I'm last in the queue. With five years I'd try to move in year two, not year four.

say: **Five years** is enough to plan if governments start now.
I'd tell everyone at the studio to think about **what they'd do instead**.
think: Five years is a **decent run** to copy what works from better drummers.
By 2031 I want to **teach properly**, with a qualification.
do: Start a part-time **teaching qualification** two evenings a week next year.
Use the **studio's AI tools** once Marcus sets them up.
Build savings to **a full year** of both partners' costs.
feel: **Anxious but steadier**, like seeing a storm two days out.
S3.quote: Jo (the studio engineer) has spent fifteen years learning to mix, and mixing is the first thing AGI does well.
fieldNote: He knows his **habit of waiting** and sets himself an earlier deadline.
His worry for **Jo** shows he sees desk work as first in line.
Teaching with a **qualification** is his chosen landing place.

steps.text: Start a part-time music teaching qualification two evenings a week
Use the studio's AI tools once Marcus installs them
Build savings to cover a full year of household costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do this right: retraining funds, union deals, rules on what's fake. That's the message I'd share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it means I can grow into a proper musician and a proper teacher before it lands. By 2036 I'd be 37, teaching in schools, playing gigs at weekends. It's still the same end point, which bothers me, but there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the teaching qualification over two or three years without rushing. I'd keep the studio as long as it pays and learn the tools when they're standard. We'd probably have kids later in the decade, so I'd want the flat mostly paid off by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. Not scared, but it sits in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might have kids later. Does this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I'd want to be sure one of us has steady work before we do. Priya's job feels safer than mine, so it'd probably depend on her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use them. Set up retraining with real money behind it, not a website. And make sure robots in schools don't replace teachers, because that's where I'm heading.

say: **Ten years** is time for retraining funds, union deals and rules on fakes.
This is the moment to **do it right**, and I'd share that.
think: I can grow into a **proper teacher** before AGI lands.
The **same end point** still bothers me, even with time.
do: Finish the **teaching qualification** over two or three years.
Learn studio AI tools once they're **standard**.
Pay most of the **flat** off before having kids.
feel: **Uneasy**, sitting quietly in the back of his head.
S4.quote: Set up retraining with real money behind it, not a website.
fieldNote: With a decade, his own route into **school teaching** feels secure enough.
**Family plans** now hinge on whose job is steadier.
He wants **real retraining money**, not a token gesture.

steps.text: Finish a music teaching qualification at a steady pace
Pay most of the flat off before starting a family
Learn the studio's AI tools once they become standard

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd go from studio drummer to wondering what I'm for in two years. What would help is a basic income while people retrain, paid for by the AI firms, and free teaching qualifications for people like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids I teach. Some of them want to be drummers, and I don't know what to tell their parents now. I'd still say learn it. Playing drums with other people is a joy you can't download, and I'd still tell my pupils to learn.

headlineQuote: Playing drums with other people is a joy you can't download, and I'd still tell my pupils to learn.
portrait: Gareth is a 27-year-old **junior house drummer** at a recording studio who teaches three evenings a week.
He and Priya, a maths teacher, own a flat and he has **eight months** saved.
He uses AI **now and then** and adopts tools once others have proved them.
He expects **studio work** to go first and plans to land in qualified teaching.
His politics push for a **basic income** and AI firms paying musicians.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his studio work would vanish within two years.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** during retraining, funded by AI firms.
Free **teaching qualifications** for musicians changing course.
